Explanation: With main (I), the verb honā (to be) is always hūṅ and goes at the very end of the sentence.
ExplanationDetail: SOV order: Main (I) + chhātra (student) + hūṅ (am).
Notes: Japanese parallel: exact same verb-final order as 私は学生です (Watashi wa gakusei desu). Hindi has no articles (no 'a' or 'the').

Explanation: For any singular 3rd-person subject (he, she, it, this, that), honā is hai.
ExplanationDetail: yah (this) + achchhī (good, f.) + kitāb (book, f.) + hai (is).
Notes: Notice gender agreement just like Spanish: kitāb is feminine, so achchhā becomes achchhī.

Explanation: Polite āp (like Spanish usted), ham (we), and plural subjects all take nasalized haiṅ.
ExplanationDetail: hūṅ (I) / hai (sg.) / ho (tum) / haiṅ (ham, āp, plural).
Notes: Politeness tip: āp always uses plural grammar (kaise haiṅ), even when talking to one person.

Explanation: Place nahīṅ (not) directly before the final verb to negate a sentence.
ExplanationDetail: Main (I) + āj (today) + thakā (tired, m.) + nahīṅ hūṅ (am not).
Notes: For a female speaker, thakā changes to thakī (Main āj thakī nahīṅ hūṅ).

SentenceEnglish: I am at home / in the house.
Explanation: Hindi uses postpositions AFTER the noun: ghar meṅ literally means 'house in'.
ExplanationDetail: Main (I) + ghar meṅ (house-in) + hūṅ (am).
Notes: Japanese parallel: ghar meṅ works exactly like 家に / 家の中に — the location marker comes right after the noun.

SentenceEnglish: The book is on the table.
Explanation: Par follows the noun to mean 'on' (a surface) or 'at' (a point/place).
ExplanationDetail: Kitāb (book) + mez par (table-on) + hai (is).
Notes: Japanese parallel: mez par mirrors テーブルの上に. Notice mez (table) is even a cognate with Spanish mesa (via Portuguese)!

Explanation: Se follows a noun to mean 'from' (origin/starting point), 'with' (instrument), or 'by' (transport).
ExplanationDetail: Main (I) + Meksiko se (Mexico-from) + hūṅ (am).
Notes: Japanese parallel: Meksiko se = メキシコから (kara). It also covers 'by train' (ṭren se = 電車で).

Explanation: Ke liye is a compound postposition meaning 'for' (a person or purpose).
ExplanationDetail: āp ke liye (for you) / mere liye (for me, fused form).
Notes: Japanese parallel: āp ke liye maps directly onto あなたのために (no tame ni).

Explanation: Merā (my) agrees in gender and number with the OWNED noun: nām is masculine singular → merā.
ExplanationDetail: merā (m. sg.) / merī (f. sg./pl.) / mere (m. pl. or oblique).
Notes: Spanish parallel: just like nuestro / nuestra agrees with the possessed object, merā / merī / mere agrees with what is owned, never the speaker.

Explanation: Before any feminine noun (singular or plural), 'my' is always merī.
ExplanationDetail: merī kitāb (my book) / merī bahan (my sister) / merī kitābeṅ (my books).
Notes: A great rule of thumb: most Hindi nouns ending in -ī (and common words like kitāb, chāy, bāt) are feminine.

Pattern: Owner + kā (m. sg.) / kī (f.) / ke (m. pl.) + Owned
Explanation: Kā / kī / ke links Owner + Owned (just like Japanese の), and agrees with the OWNED noun (ghar = m. sg. → kā).
ExplanationDetail: Rām kā ghar (Ram's house, m.) vs. Rām kī bahan (Ram's sister, f.).
Notes: Japanese + Spanish hybrid: order is Japanese (Rām kā ghar = ラムの家), agreement is Spanish (m. kā / f. kī).

Explanation: Before a masculine plural noun (dost here is plural because of ve … haiṅ), merā becomes mere.
ExplanationDetail: merā dost (my friend) → mere dost (my friends).
Notes: Notice dost doesn't change spelling in plural, so mere and haiṅ tell you it's plural.

Explanation: Masculine nouns ending in -ā change to -e (oblique case) whenever followed by any postposition (meṅ, par, se, ko).
ExplanationDetail: kamrā (room) → kamre meṅ (in the room); laṛkā (boy) → laṛke ko (to the boy).
Notes: This is one of Hindi's core rules: postposition triggers oblique (-ā → -e on the noun and its adjectives: baṛe kamre meṅ).

Pattern: merā / baṛā → mere / baṛe before postposition
SentenceEnglish: There is a garden in my house.
Explanation: Even when the noun is singular (ghar), a following postposition (meṅ) turns merā into oblique mere.
ExplanationDetail: merā ghar (my house) → mere ghar meṅ (in my house).
Notes: Feminine merī never changes in oblique (merī kitāb meṅ); only masculine -ā shifts to -e.

Explanation: Main (I) + ko (to) fuses into the high-frequency dative pronoun mujhe («to me»).
ExplanationDetail: You'll use mujhe constantly for 'to me', 'I like' (mujhe pasand hai), and 'I need' (mujhe chāhiye).
Notes: Spanish parallel: mujhe behaves a lot like Spanish me / a mí.

GrammarPoint: Dative polite you: āp + ko → āpko
Pattern: āp + ko → āpko / tum + ko → tumheṅ
Explanation: Polite āp attaches ko directly to form āpko («to you»).
ExplanationDetail: Key dative pronouns: mujhe (to me), tumheṅ (to you), āpko (to you, polite), use (to him/her).
Notes: Literally: 'To-you what is-needed?' — exact same structure as Spanish ¿qué le hace falta?

Explanation: Drop -nā from the infinitive (pīnā → pī-) and add -tā (m. sg.) + hūṅ for daily habits.
ExplanationDetail: SOV: Main (I) + roz (every day) + chāy (tea) + pītā hūṅ (drink).
Notes: Japanese parallel: Main roz chāy pītā hūṅ = 毎日お茶を飲みます.

SentenceEnglish: She reads a book every night.
Sentence: वह हर रात किताब पढ़ती है।
Explanation: For any feminine subject (singular or plural), add -tī to the verb stem + hai/haiṅ.
ExplanationDetail: paṛhnā (to read/study) → stem paṛh- + -tī hai.
Notes: Notice how Hindi has no separate 'he' vs 'she' pronoun (both are vah) — the verb ending -tā / -tī tells you the gender!

Explanation: Masculine plural, mixed groups, and polite āp take stem + -te + haiṅ.
ExplanationDetail: bolnā (to speak) → bol- + -te haiṅ. Same for āp: Āp Hindī bolte haiṅ?
Notes: Habitual endings mirror the possessive pattern: -tā (m. sg.), -tī (f.), -te (m. pl. / polite).

Explanation: In negative habitual sentences, Hindi normally drops the final hūṅ / hai / haiṅ.
ExplanationDetail: Main māṅs khātā hūṅ (I eat meat) → Main māṅs nahīṅ khātā (I don't eat meat).
Notes: Natural spoken Hindi almost always drops hūṅ/hai after nahīṅ + -tā/-tī/-te (adding it sounds emphatic).

SentenceEnglish: I am going to the market right now. (m.)
Sentence: मैं अभी बाज़ार जा रहा हूँ।
Explanation: For an action happening right now, use verb stem + rahā (m. sg.) / rahī (f.) / rahe (m. pl.) + honā.
ExplanationDetail: jānā (to go) → stem jā + rahā hūṅ.
Notes: Japanese parallel: jā rahā hūṅ corresponds to 〜ている (行っています) for ongoing actions.

Explanation: With a feminine subject, the continuous marker changes from rahā to rahī.
ExplanationDetail: sonā (to sleep) → stem so + rahī hai.
Notes: Unlike French (which uses en train de), Hindi uses rahā/rahī/rahe constantly — just like Spanish está durmiendo.

Explanation: For plural / mixed groups and polite āp, use verb stem + rahe + haiṅ.
ExplanationDetail: sīkhnā (to learn) → sīkh + rahe haiṅ.
Notes: Notice the exact same 3-way ending everywhere in Hindi: -ā (m. sg.), -ī (f.), -e (m. pl. / polite).

GrammarPoint: Question word in situ (kyā kar rahe ho?)
Explanation: Hindi question words (kyā, kahāṅ, kab) stay right before the verb in SOV order — they don't jump to the front.
ExplanationDetail: Tum (you) + kyā (what) + kar rahe ho (are doing).
Notes: Japanese parallel: exact same in-situ question word order as 何をしていますか (Nani o shite imasu ka)!

Explanation: To say 'I like X', put the person in dative (mujhe) + X + pasand hai (singular) or pasand haiṅ (plural).
ExplanationDetail: Literally: 'To-me coffee pleasing is.'
Notes: Triple bridge! Hindi Mujhe kŏfī pasand hai = Spanish Me gusta el café = Japanese 私はコーヒーが好きです.

Explanation: Chāhiye is an invariable form meaning 'is needed / wanted' — it never takes hūṅ or hai after it.
ExplanationDetail: Mujhe (to me) + thoṛā pānī (a little water) + chāhiye (is needed).
Notes: Japanese parallel: Mujhe pānī chāhiye mirrors 水が欲しいです. For plural objects you can also hear chāhiyeṅ.

Sentence: मैं दफ़्तर में काम करता हूँ।
Explanation: Hundreds of Hindi verbs are built as Noun + karnā (to do), where only karnā conjugates.
ExplanationDetail: kām (work) + karnā (do) → kām kartā hūṅ (I work).
Notes: Japanese parallel: kām karnā is the exact twin of 仕事をする (shigoto o suru) — noun + 'do'!

Sentence: मैं अभी काम शुरू कर रहा हूँ।
SentenceCloze: Main abhī kām {{c1::shurū kar rahā hūṅ}}.
Explanation: Shurū (beginning) + karnā (do) means 'to start'; conjugate karnā into any tense (kar rahā hūṅ = am starting).
ExplanationDetail: Other essential karnā verbs: bāt karnā (talk), intazār karnā (wait), madad karnā (help), koshish karnā (try).
Notes: Just like Japanese する-verbs (開始する, 勉強する), learning karnā unlocks huge chunks of Hindi vocabulary immediately.

Explanation: With tum (friendly/informal 'you', like Spanish tú), honā is always ho.
ExplanationDetail: main → hūṅ | yah/vah → hai | tum → ho | āp/ham/ve → haiṅ.
Notes: Question order: kahāṅ (where) stays right before the verb, just like Japanese どこにいますか.

Explanation: Putting kyā at the very start of any statement turns it into a yes/no question without changing word order.
ExplanationDetail: Yah chāy garm hai (This tea is hot) → Kyā yah chāy garm hai? (Is this tea hot?).
Notes: Japanese parallel: kyā at the start plays the exact same role as か (ka) at the end of a Japanese sentence!

Explanation: Vah (often pronounced 'vo' in everyday speech) means 'he', 'she', 'it', or 'that'.
ExplanationDetail: yah ('ye') = this / he / she (near) | vah ('vo') = that / he / she (far).
Notes: In spoken Hindi, almost everyone says vo for vah and ye for yah — you'll hear it in the TTS audio!

Explanation: Put nahīṅ right before hai to negate an adjective or noun statement.
ExplanationDetail: Yah (this) + muśkil (difficult) + nahīṅ hai (is not).
Notes: Opposites to remember together: āsān (easy) vs. muśkil (difficult).

SentenceEnglish: I am at the office until evening.
Sentence: मैं शाम तक दफ़्तर में हूँ।
Explanation: Tak follows a time or place noun to mean 'until' or 'as far as / up to'.
ExplanationDetail: śām tak (until evening) / kal tak (until tomorrow) / station tak (up to the station).
Notes: Japanese parallel: se … tak (from … until) is the exact twin of Japanese から … まで (kara … made)!

SentenceEnglish: I am at home with a friend.
Sentence: मैं दोस्त के साथ घर में हूँ।
SentenceCloze: Main dost {{c1::ke sāth}} ghar meṅ hūṅ.
Explanation: Ke sāth is a compound postposition meaning 'with / together with' a person.
ExplanationDetail: dost ke sāth (with a friend) / mere sāth (with me) / āpke sāth (with you).
Notes: Japanese parallel: dost ke sāth = 友達と / 友達と一緒に.

Explanation: Hindi has no verb 'to have' for possessions: use [Owner] + ke pās (literally 'near me') + [Object] + hai.
ExplanationDetail: main + ke pās → mere pās | āp + ke pās → āpke pās | Rām ke pās.
Notes: Japanese parallel: works like 私には時間があります (existence at a person) rather than a transitive 'have' verb.

Sentence: मैं काम के बाद खाली हूँ।
Explanation: Ke bād follows a noun to mean 'after'; its opposite is ke pahle ('before').
ExplanationDetail: kām ke bād (after work) vs. kām ke pahle (before work).
Notes: Japanese parallel: kām ke bād = 仕事の後で (shigoto no ato de).

Explanation: Even though Ram is male, kī agrees with bahan (sister, feminine) — the OWNED noun.
ExplanationDetail: Rām kā bhāī (Ram's brother, m.) vs. Rām kī bahan (Ram's sister, f.).
Notes: Always look forward at the noun after kā/kī/ke to pick its gender — never backward at the owner.

Explanation: Before a masculine plural owned noun (dost = friends), kā becomes ke.
ExplanationDetail: Rām kā dost (Ram's friend) → Rām ke dost (Ram's friends).
Notes: Full trio: kā (m. sg.), kī (f. sg./pl.), ke (m. pl. or oblique).

Explanation: Āp + kā fuses into āpkā (agreeing with masculine singular nām).
ExplanationDetail: āpkā nām (your name, m.) / āpkī kitāb (your book, f.) / āpke dost (your friends, m. pl.).
Notes: Notice how kyā ('what') sits right before hai: literally 'Your name what is?' (お名前は何ですか).

Explanation: Vah (he/she) becomes oblique us- before kā/kī/ke → uskā (m. sg.), uskī (f.), uske (m. pl.).
ExplanationDetail: gāṛī (car/vehicle) is feminine, so both uskī and naī (new, f.) take -ī.
Notes: Hindi doesn't distinguish 'his' vs. 'her' — uskī means both, and agrees only with gāṛī (car).

SentenceEnglish: I give a book to the boy. (m.)
Sentence: मैं लड़के को किताब देता हूँ।
Explanation: Before the recipient postposition ko ('to'), masculine laṛkā (boy) shifts to oblique laṛke.
ExplanationDetail: Main (I) + laṛke ko (to the boy) + kitāb (book) + detā hūṅ (give).
Notes: Japanese parallel: laṛke ko = 男の子に (indirect object marker ni).

SentenceEnglish: We live in a big city.
Sentence: हम बड़े शहर में रहते हैं।
Explanation: Even though śahar (city) doesn't end in -ā and stays unchanged, its adjective baṛā (big) still turns into oblique baṛe before meṅ.
ExplanationDetail: baṛā śahar (a big city) → baṛe śahar meṅ (in a big city).
Notes: Every -ā word inside a postpositional phrase (possessive, adjective, noun) shifts to -e together.

Sentence: मैं दोस्तों के साथ जा रहा हूँ।
SentenceCloze: Main {{c1::dostoṅ}} ke sāth jā rahā hūṅ.
Explanation: Almost ALL plural nouns (both masculine and feminine!) end in -oṅ when followed by a postposition.
ExplanationDetail: dost → dostoṅ ke sāth (with friends) | kitāb → kitāboṅ meṅ (in books) | ghar → gharoṅ meṅ (in houses).
Notes: One of the cleanest rules in Hindi: plural + postposition = -oṅ (dostoṅ, laṛkoṅ, kitāboṅ).

Explanation: Vah (he/she) + ko contracts to use (or usko) meaning 'to him / to her'.
ExplanationDetail: Dative set: mujhe (to me), tumheṅ (to you), āpko (to you, polite), use (to him/her), hameṅ (to us).
Notes: Spanish parallel: use = le / a él / a ella (Le gusta la música).

Explanation: Rahnā ('to live / stay') uses habitual present for where you reside: stem rah- + -tā hūṅ.
ExplanationDetail: Main (I) + Dillī meṅ (in Delhi) + rahtā hūṅ (live).
Notes: Notice rahnā is the same verb behind the continuous marker rahā/rahī/rahe!

SentenceEnglish: She goes to the office every day.
Explanation: Jānā ('to go') drops -nā to stem jā- and takes -tī hai for a feminine subject.
ExplanationDetail: Notice destination daftar often needs no postposition before jānā (daftar jānā = go to the office).
Notes: Contrast with continuous: daftar jātī hai (goes every day) vs. daftar jā rahī hai (is going right now).

Explanation: Samajhnā ('to understand') forms regular habitual present: samajh- + -tā hūṅ (f.: samajhtī hūṅ).
ExplanationDetail: All language names (Hindī, Jāpānī, Frāṅsīsī) are feminine, so thoṛā → thoṛī Hindī.
Notes: Survival negative: Main nahīṅ samajhtā (m.) / Main nahīṅ samajhtī (f.) = 'I don't understand.'

Explanation: Polite āp takes stem + -te haiṅ (for a male or general addressee) and -tī haiṅ (for a female addressee).
ExplanationDetail: Kyā (yes/no) + āp (you, polite) + chāy (tea) + pīte haiṅ (drink).
Notes: Compare polite Kyā āp chāy pīte haiṅ? with friendly Kyā tum chāy pīte ho?

SentenceEnglish: I am eating food right now. (m.)
Sentence: मैं अभी खाना खा रहा हूँ।
Explanation: Khānā works as both noun ('food') and verb ('to eat'): khānā khā rahā hūṅ = 'am eating food'.
ExplanationDetail: abhī ('right now') pairs naturally with the continuous tense.
Notes: Japanese parallel: khānā khā rahā hūṅ mirrors ご飯を食べています (gohan o tabete imasu).

Explanation: Dekhnā ('to see / watch / look') takes stem dekh + rahe haiṅ with ham (we).
ExplanationDetail: Ham (we) + film (movie) + dekh rahe haiṅ (are watching).
Notes: Just like Japanese 見る (miru), dekhnā covers 'see', 'watch', and 'look at'.

Explanation: Likhnā ('to write') drops -nā to likh and takes rahī hai for a feminine subject.
ExplanationDetail: Continuous never changes the verb stem itself — only rahā / rahī / rahe + honā changes!
Notes: That makes Hindi continuous super easy: once you know the stem (likh, paṛh, dekh, bol), you can form it instantly.

Pattern: bāriś (f.) + ho rahī hai («it is raining»)
Explanation: Literally 'outside rain is happening': bāriś (rain) is feminine, so honā becomes ho rahī hai.
ExplanationDetail: Hindi uses [weather noun] + ho rahā/rahī hai instead of a dummy 'it'.
Notes: Japanese parallel: 'rain is happening' mirrors Japanese 雨が降っています (no dummy 'it' subject).

Explanation: To say you know a language or skill, Hindi literally says 'it comes to me' (ānā): Hindī (f.) → ātī hai.
ExplanationDetail: Mujhe Hindī ātī hai (I know Hindi) / Mujhe tairnā ātā hai (I know how to swim).
Notes: Notice the verb agrees with Hindī (feminine → ātī hai), NOT with the speaker!

Explanation: Physical feelings (hunger, thirst, cold) use dative mujhe + feeling + lagnā ('to strike/attach').
ExplanationDetail: bhūkh (hunger, f.) → lagī hai | pyās (thirst, f.) → Mujhe pyās lagī hai ('I am thirsty').
Notes: Spanish bridge: neither Spanish (tengo hambre) nor Hindi (mujhe bhūkh lagī hai) uses 'I am' for hunger!

Sentence: हम हिंदी में बात कर रहे हैं।
SentenceCloze: Ham Hindī meṅ {{c1::bāt kar rahe haiṅ}}.
Explanation: Bāt (talk/matter) + karnā (do) is the standard verb for 'to talk / have a conversation'.
ExplanationDetail: Ham (we) + Hindī meṅ (in Hindi) + bāt kar rahe haiṅ (are talking).
Notes: Japanese parallel: bāt karnā = 話をする (hanashi o suru).

Pattern: [Person] + kī madad karnā («to do someone's help»)
Sentence: मैं उसकी मदद कर रहा हूँ।
Explanation: Madad (help, f.) + karnā (do) means 'to help', and takes kī with the person helped (uskī madad = 'his/her help').
ExplanationDetail: Main (I) + uskī (his/her, f. agreeing with madad) + madad kar rahā hūṅ (am helping).
Notes: Notice how kī connects us- to madad (f.), literally 'doing his/her help' — a super common Hindi pattern!
